content.thinking:
I notice there's an existing koala.ts in the sandbox samples directory, but I'll leave that alone since I'm writing a separate koalaSonnet.ts file. I need to test running commands in that directory, checking whether npm works there, then start designing the koala gripping a eucalyptus branch stand at roughly real scale.

For the pose I'm picturing a base plinth with a mounted eucalyptus branch at a slight angle, complete with side branches and leaf cards, and the koala clinging to the main trunk with all four limbs wrapped around it, arms stretched forward and legs to the sides so the belly rests against the bark while the head turns outward toward the viewer.

I'm now working through where exactly the trunk sits relative to the koala's body and leaning toward a simpler fork composition: the koala sitting upright on a horizontal branch with legs spread over it, arms gripping a diagonal branch rising in front of its chest, face peeking out beside it. I'm sketching the base dimensions and starting the trunk's vertical sweep from there.

Let me try a simpler setup instead: koala sitting in a Y-fork, with the two branches rising left and right like a V, and the arms wrapping around each branch respectively.

I'm placing the arms gripping the branches near the shoulders, roughly at (±0.17, 0.72, 0.1), with the torso centered around (0, 0.5, 0), sized about 0.13 wide and 0.45 tall for a seated koala roughly 0.6m high.

Working out proportions: rump at y≈0.42, chest top ~0.72, head center ~0.82 with a wide head (~0.2) and ears, topping out near 0.93 plus ears, giving the koala itself about 0.75m tall while the branch stand pushes total height to around 1.4m. I'm also reconsidering the branch structure, leaning toward a V-fork trunk rising from a base rather than a single vertical limb, to keep the eucalyptus setup looking natural.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton: hip root, a short spine chain rising to the chest and neck, then a head joint positioned forward and up for the big rounded koala head with its characteristic large ears, oversized leathery nose, and pale chin. For the hind legs I'm placing hips, forward-angled knees, and feet gripping the trunk fork just below the crotch, working out exact joint coordinates so the koala looks like it's naturally clinging to the branch.

Still working out branch curve positions...

Hands grip the branch around y≈0.65–0.7 at x=±0.215, with elbows bent given the shorter chest-to-hand span, and paws designed as chunky wrapped digits with opposable thumbs and small claw cones in a pixel-art style. Hind feet grip a lower point on the branches near y≈0.46.

Now I'm working out the hip and knee placement for a sitting posture, with hips around (±0.1,0.4) and knees bent forward-out so the legs fold naturally toward a foot resting on the branch fork rather than dangling awkwardly — testing whether raising the feet higher on the branch looks more natural for a sitting koala.

I'm defining the branch as a curved path using control points for the trunk and forked limbs, with varying tube radii, then figuring out where along that curve to anchor the hands so they wrap around the branch surface near where the shoulders would naturally reach.

That bend seems too extreme, so I'm widening the fork and shortening the reach—placing the hands farther out at roughly x=±0.3, which brings the shoulder-to-hand distance down to a manageable range and lets the elbow drop out and slightly down for a more natural pose.

For depth, I'm placing the branch slightly forward in z so the koala's hands wrap around it naturally, with the crotch and trunk set a bit behind at negative z for that gripping pose.

Now I'm sketching the body proportions — a pear-shaped trunk that's wider at the hips, tapering toward the chest, built from a series of radius stations lofted along the spine curve.

For the surface treatment, I'm planning a pixel-art style with dithered grey fur ramps, choosing a texel size fine enough to resolve the koala's head and facial features without looking too blocky.

I'm checking that the paint resolution works out with a 2048 paint size across the model's surface area, landing around 1mm texels, so cells around 1.5cm will read as clean pixel-art detail. For the overall head shape, I'm thinking a simplified squashed sphere with low segment count to keep that chunky pixel-art look.

For the body, I'm leaning toward faceted low-poly sweeps (8-sided, flat-shaded) rather than smooth rounded forms to better match the hard-edged pixel aesthetic, while still letting cellPaint keep its square texel grid on curved surfaces. Now I'm sketching out the koala's color palette, starting with grey fur and a lighter belly tone.

For fur detail I'm thinking of dithered grey ramps plus pixel-textured cards for ear tufts, cheek fluff, and chest fur, alongside eucalyptus leaf cards using a few pixel-leaf texture variants. For the ears, I'm weighing a flattened sphere with a separate pixel-textured inner-tuft plane versus a stepped-outline extruded disc colored via cellPaint to get that rounded, flattened koala ear shape.

Working out ear geometry now, using stepped circular outlines (outer base plus smaller inner fluff layer) sized to about 0.144 diameter with 0.03 thickness. For the nose I'm planning a dark rounded box with a highlighted pixel tile on the front/top, a paler small box for the muzzle beneath it, and tiny 2x2 pixel eyes with a single white highlight placed close together to match a koala's face.

Now I'm detailing the mouth as a separate upper/lower jaw structure, with a pixel-drawn mouth line texture on the head, plus claws rendered as bone-colored cones -- syndactyl fused toes with a grooming claw on the hind feet, and five-digit forepaws with two opposable digits. I'm also tallying up the joint count across spine, neck, head, jaw, ears, arms, and digits to make sure the total stays under the 160 joint limit, landing around 60.

For the finger-wrapping grip around the branch, I'm working out how each digit should curl as a two-segment chain in a plane perpendicular to the branch axis, with digits 1-2 wrapping from one side and 3-5 from the other to mimic a real koala's grip, figuring out how they stack along the vertical branch.

Still working out finger positioning...

Feet follow a similar pattern on lower branches, with toe arcs around the branch; biologically, koalas have a clawless opposable big toe on hind feet with the second and third toes fused together sharing two claws, so I'll model five toes with the big toe clawless and toes 2-3 grouped together.

For legs, the koala sits upright with thighs spreading from hips to feet planted on the lower branch. I'm positioning the hip joints and working out where the ankle meets the branch, aiming for a natural squatting posture with knees jutting forward rather than hand-computing exact coordinates now—better to let the branch function determine foot placement in code.

I'm building the leg chain with a hip-knee-ankle structure using a forward bend hint, then attaching foot geometry and toe joints parented at the ankle so the feet can wrap around the branch.

For the tail, I'll just add a tiny rump stub since koalas barely have one. Then I'm planning fur details using textured cards for cheek fluff, ear tufts, and chest tufts, with a small pixelated tuft texture applied across a pixel-art atlas for that fringed look.

For the eucalyptus tree, I'm thinking through bark color palettes with cream, pinkish-grey, and olive patches, plus peeling bark ribbons as curled textured cards, and sickle-shaped blue-green leaves typical of eucalyptus.

For the base/stand, I'm designing a pixel wooden plinth from stacked plank-textured boxes, topped with moss and grass cellPaint plus small rock boxes and tufts.

Working through the proportions: branches reaching up to about 1.4m including leaves, total height near 1.45m with the plinth, and the trunk rising from the base to a crotch around 0.3m where the koala sits. Checking that against real koala proportions, a seated body height of roughly 0.6m from seat to ear-tip looks right, and I'm placing the trunk slightly behind the koala's body along the z-axis for a natural perch.

Now I'm setting up coordinate conventions, naming joints like hipL for the model's left side, and building out the color palette -- a fur gradient of six grayscale tones, a cream under-belly ramp, and darker nose colors.

Still writing palette...

I'm applying that same fur paint logic to arms and legs, adding subtle speckling and a dappled rump patch with brown streaks for realism. Now I'm shifting to building the skeleton, defining the spine chain as a sequence of joints curving from the hips upward through the torso.

Making the neck a single joint, then attaching the head as a rigid bone placed by absolute world coordinates for simplicity, since the body parts are axis-aligned shapes that don't need local rotation. Moving on to building the body sweep with its path and radius function.

I'm working out which bones drive the body's chain -- deciding whether hips should duplicate the spine's starting joint or just extend the sweep path from the rump up to the shoulders using the existing spine chain.

For the sweep's round caps, I'm calculating where the rump's bottom should sink below the hips joint so the seat makes contact with the ground plane, settling on hips around y=0.47 with a rump radius that puts the bottom near y=0.33.

For the body width, I'm tapering the radius along the sweep so hips are widest, the belly pear-shape bulges a bit more around t=0.3, then narrows toward the shoulders since koalas have narrower shoulders than belly. The neck will be a short thick sweep merging into the head, and I'm sizing the head wide and round like a chibi koala with its own width, height, and depth values.

Now I'm placing the head shape as a scaled sphere with a forward muzzle bump and a large oval black nose typical of a koala's spade-shaped nose, then positioning small bead-like eyes close to the nose near the front of the face.

I'm also considering a pixelated face plate texture layered over the front of the head to add eye detail, eyebrow fuzz, mouth lines, nose shading, and cheek highlights, rather than modeling each feature separately.

I'm placing the jaw joint and sizing the upper and lower jaw pieces, with a thin dark seam box to suggest the mouth line between them. Now I'm figuring out the ear geometry as a stepped-disc extrusion positioned symmetrically on the head.

Still working out ear tilt math...

Working out the correct outward normal and extrusion axes so both sides of the ear face outward consistently, then planning the inner ear as a smaller cream disc with a fluffy white rim outline.

For the ear structure, I'm going with a grey outer back disc, a cream/white front disc offset slightly along the normal for fuzz, and placing the ears at roughly (±0.115, 0.925, 0.03) with a radius of about 0.065, then moving on to planning cheek fluff cards.

For the cheek tufts, I'm scattering small pale cards along the sides and lower face of the head sphere, leaning them at 60 degrees with sizes around 0.03-0.04 to get a textured tuft effect. Then I'm extending that same fur-card approach across the whole body, using roughly 250 small grey tufts, before shifting to the arm rig with shoulder-elbow-wrist joint chains positioned near (±0.125, 0.70, 0.03).

Now I'm defining the limb function so three joint names map to hip, knee, and ankle points along the leg chain, and working out the branch curve as a set of catmull-rom control points sweeping upward in y with slight z offsets, checking that the branch radius near y=0.4-0.5 sits close enough to the body's hip width that the hind feet and toes can wrap naturally around it.

Figuring out where the foot actually sits relative to the branch center causes an overlap problem -- the ankle position ends up buried inside the belly volume since the body's cross-section extends further than expected at that height. I need to widen the hip stance and push the branch path outward at lower y-values so the legs and feet remain visible outside the torso instead of hidden beneath it.

Computing the triangle height gives knee offset about 0.16 from the hip-ankle line, confirming the knee juts forward as intended — consistent with a koala resting in a frog-sit posture. I'll set the knee hint direction accordingly.

Now working through the arm geometry: placing the shoulder joint, finding the branch contact point, and solving the triangle for the elbow fold so the wrist lands at the inner-front grip point on the branch, using the same law-of-cosines approach as the legs.

With the koala's head reaching up to 0.95 and branches spread at ±0.37, there's room around the head for foliage. I'm thinking of adding twig clusters curving inward from each branch around y 1.15-1.35 to form a canopy arching above the head.

For the trunk, I'm defining a path from the plinth top (y=0.07) up through a fork where the branches split, with radius tapering from 0.08 down to 0.035, plus a joint sphere covering the crotch. Since full skeletons are required for animals but branches are rigid props, I'm figuring the branch meshes should just weight to the nearest existing joint rather than getting their own bones.

Actually, I realize this creates a problem: if hands grip the branch and weight to wrist joints, flexing the koala's arms would awkwardly drag parts of the branch along with them. I think the cleaner solution is to give the stand its own rigid joint hierarchy, separate from the koala's arm bones, accepting that hands may visually separate slightly from the branch during animation. I'm restructuring so a new root joint "base" sits at the plinth, with hips becoming its child, keeping the stand's joints as a distinct rigid chain rather than folding everything under the koala's skeleton.

Now I'm laying out the spine, neck, and head joints with their positions and aim directions, then deciding how the arms and legs attach to the spine and hips, before sweeping the body geometry along the spine path with the assigned bone weights.

I'm also working out the rump dome shape and crotch positioning so the lower body geometry fits cleanly against the branch radius without overlapping incorrectly.

Hips sit at the bottom of the body with the thigh joints as children, which checks out, and I'm placing a small tail nub joint with its own fur part. For the ears I'll add hinge joints under the head for flopping motion, but I'll skip separate eye joints since eyelids are too minor to warrant their own skeleton nodes.

Now I'm working out the hand geometry, finding where the branch path meets the wrist height and using the tangent there to orient each finger's rotation axis, with the digit arcs curving based on handedness and a palm direction computed toward the front-inner side.

Confirming that positive rotation about the +Y axis increases θ, so for the left branch fingers 3-5 wrap with positive φ about that axis; for the mirrored right side, the same logic applies starting from the opposite base angle.

Now thinking about the thumb digits (1,2), which wrap in the opposite direction from fingers 3-5, starting near the inner-back of the palm.

Working out finger geometry: with radius near 0.05m and a 130° sweep, each finger comes out around 0.113m long, which fits a koala's proportionally long digits, using tube radius 0.011. For stacking the five digits along the branch axis, I'm spacing three fingers and two opposing thumbs at small offsets so they interleave realistically around the branch.

I'm sorting out so the fingers and thumbs occupy non-overlapping angular ranges (fingers sweeping the front, thumbs the inner side) while sharing a common palm origin, then building the palm as a capsule connecting the wrist point to the digits' shared start, positioning the wrist slightly farther from the branch surface than the digit bases for a natural grip shape.

Now I'm naming the digit joint chains for each hand (thumb, index, middle, ring, pinky, each with two segments) and mirroring that approach for the hind feet, where the big toe acts like an opposable thumb without a claw while toes 2-3 fuse together and 4-5 wrap around the front like the fingers.

I'm also tallying up the total joint count across the base, hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, ears, tail, arms, hand digits, legs, and toe digits to confirm everything sums to 63. Next I need to set up the fur tuft scattering across body surfaces and start writing the texture code.

Designing the eucalyptus leaf pixel texture requires balancing texel resolution against card size -- I'm working out that leaf cards need finer pixel density than the body paint texture, settling on something like 6-10 pixels wide to keep the texel scale consistent with the overall 0.012m body cell resolution.

I'm planning three leaf color variants (blue-green, olive, reddish new-growth), small fur tuft textures for white and grey patches, and a face decal sized to fit the head sphere's front region.

For the face decal, I'm mapping out pixel positions for the eyes (dark with a light highlight), lighter brow smudges above each eye, darker fur rims around the eyes, cheek fluff details, and a mouth line beneath the muzzle.

I realize the mouth should actually sit on the separate muzzle/jaw box, so the face decal stops where the muzzle begins. I'm considering using `b.decal()` to apply the texture onto the head part's skin at the right position, direction, and size, then designing a small pixel-art nose texture sized to fit the nose box's front face dimensions with black coloring and a darker rim highlight.

For the nose I want nostril marks plus a small white highlight on the front face, and simpler crops on the top and side faces, so I'm defining a skin layout where each face of the nose box gets its own drawn region rather than tiling one texture uniformly. I'm sizing that nose box based on the pixel dimensions times my chosen texel scale to keep proportions consistent with the rest of the model, and deciding to keep the head as a simple sphere with a decal instead of building it as a skinned box, since that keeps the koala look rounder. Next I want to work on the plinth using a wood-plank tile texture with some dithering.

Now I'm planning the plinth as a layered structure: a base frame, a thin moss-painted turf slab on top, a flattened dirt mound around the trunk base, and scattered details like small rocks, grass tufts, fallen leaf cards, gumnuts, and a small brass plaque with a leaf icon on the front face. For the eucalyptus bark I'm working out a procedural streak pattern using stretched noise sampling along a squashed vertical axis to create vertical bark striations, with lighter peeling patches where the noise crosses a threshold, and darker fibrous bark lower on the trunk transitioning to smoother pale bark higher up.

I'm defining the bark color gradient by height, mixing rough grey-brown tones below with cream, sage, and dusky pink ramps on the smooth upper limbs, then designing peeling bark strips as small curled texture cards hung from branch frames to hang downward naturally. Now I'm sketching out how thin reddish twig sweeps branch off the main limbs with leaf cards placed along each twig using computed frames at intervals.

Figuring out the leaf orientation so they hang down eucalyptus-style—facing outward from the twig with a downward flow and curl bend—and planning the density: roughly 5 twigs per branch with 8-10 drooping leaf cards each, targeting around 260 leaf cards clustered mainly at branch tops and midway points.

For twig geometry, I'm working out how each twig sweeps outward and upward from its branch attachment point, tapering radius as it extends, with leaves attached along alternating clock angles on the twig's frame so they splay naturally rather than clumping on one side.

I'm thinking through adding small gumnut clusters at twig tips—tiny spheres with a lighter cap for the woody pod look—while keeping the part count cheap so the whole tree doesn't get too heavy.

Tallying parts across body, head, limbs, claws, stand, twigs, and gumnuts to make sure the total stays well under budget. Now I'm sketching out a muted color palette for the koala's fur, with cool grays for the body and a warmer cream tone for accent patches, to drive a cell-based dithered paint effect across the surface.

Writing fur paint logic...

Still refining head shading...

Still writing color logic...

I'm thinking through faceted shading for a pixel-art style, planning low-segment, non-smooth geometry for limbs and slightly higher segment count for the body to get that chunky look while staying within a limited flat color palette.

Now I'm setting up the imports I'll need for the builder, math, path, IK, and pixel-paint helpers, making sure to trim anything unused to avoid typecheck errors. Building the koala's skeleton...

Thinking about joint hierarchy next—I'm weighing whether to make "base" the root with "hips" as the first spine joint underneath, versus making hips itself the root. Keeping base as root feels more logical for animation since a child "stand" joint under hips would move whenever hips does, which isn't ideal.

Now I'm defining the spine path waypoints and a helper function for interpolating body radius along the chain, with tapering values for both x and y radii at key points from hips to chest, plus a rounded dome cap at the top of the torso.

I'm checking that the dome's top doesn't poke too far into the head sphere given their respective centers and radii, and deciding whether to add a short thick neck capsule to bridge the gap between chest and head joints, since the body dome should mostly stay hidden within the head geometry at rest pose.

Now I'm defining the head's sub-parts: a scaled, faceted sphere for the skull, small puffy cheek spheres on either side, a low-segment sphere for the upper muzzle, and starting to work out where the nose box should sit relative to the muzzle and head front faces.

Then I'm placing the lower jaw as a flattened sphere positioned below the muzzle, and planning a thin dark box to represent the mouth line between jaw and muzzle.

Maybe instead I should decal-project onto the skull and muzzle together, though jaw movement complicates weighting. Alternatively, I could use a separate small textured plane floating just in front of the muzzle to represent the mouth rather than fighting with the decal geometry.

For the mouth, I'll decal onto the muzzle surface specifically—placed slightly above its lower front with a small 12×5 px texture showing a dark curved line and philtrum detail, offset just enough to avoid z-fighting. For the eyes, I'll decal small 6×6 textures onto the skull near the brow area, symmetric on either side.

Now I'm sketching the eye pixel pattern itself—small round black pupil with a highlight dot, trying a few grid shapes until settling on a 5×5 arrangement scaled to about 0.035 size, then considering adding a subtle darker ring around it to suggest an eyelid.

For the rest of the head, I'm planning cream brow tufts above the eyes, giving the ears their own hinge-joint attachments near the top of the skull, and scattering cream fur cards around the cheeks and head sides angled to flow backward. Body parts will use the grey fur material, with the arms built from swept geometry along limb chains for smooth forearm shapes.

Now I'm working out the leg sweeps, tapering thigh-to-ankle radius along the bone chain, and figuring out how to place claw spikes at each digit tip using the chain's end frame and tangent direction for orientation.

For the claws, I realize a straight spike pointing tangentially outward would look wrong -- it should curl inward toward the branch, so I'm blending the tangent direction with an inward radial component to get the curved claw direction before placing the spike at the chain's endpoint.

For the foot digits, I'm laying out toe spikes along angular offsets around the foot radius, making the hind foot slightly larger, and defining a helper to find the branch's centerline point and tangent at any given position so I can compute grip points for hands and feet consistently.

Working out the branch radius as a function of path parameter so the hand grip points sit correctly against the tapering branch surface, interpolating radius along the path length to match where the hands land at y≈0.69.

Now I'm defining each digit's arc: computing a center point offset along the branch axis, a start vector at the current radius plus finger radius, then sweeping an arc using an axis derived from the branch tangent with sign flipped for thumbs versus fingers.

For the right thumb, axis flips with -s*T so negative φ sweeps θ from -30 to -160 along the inner side, which checks out. Now I'm working out the palm geometry — connecting the wrist capsule to the center point, figuring out how far the wrist sits along r0 compared to where the fingers begin their radius from the axis.

I'm checking the shoulder-to-wrist distance for folding the forelimb: computing wrist position, finding the vector back to the shoulder, and plugging the segment lengths into the fold-height formula to confirm the limb bends naturally. Everything checks out fine, so I'm moving on to positioning the hind feet.

This positioning puts the knees too high near chest level in a squatting pose, with the thigh visible but shin hidden under the body — I should adjust the hint to push the knee more forward and less upward to get a more natural stance.

Checking hind foot placement along the branch, the digits wrap properly without crossing the hips, so that spacing works. I'm defining hip joint positions inside the body where the thighs originate, mirroring joints across the x-axis for left/right legs, and setting up the base plinth as a wood plank tile sized to support the stand.

I'm stacking the plinth in layers: a bottom slab, a slightly smaller upper slab, then a moss-covered turf slab on top, adjusting trunk base height to sit flush above that stack. Checking scale, the 0.8-wide plinth feels proportionate against a koala roughly 0.6m seat-to-ear with branches included, and total stand height around 1.45 seems reasonable.

Now I'm adding ground detail—a small soil mound at the trunk base with simple segments, a few root buttresses flaring outward in bark color, low-poly rocks with flat painted stone texture, scattered grass blade cards, a couple tiny mushrooms with dotted caps, and fallen eucalyptus leaf cards lying flat on the turf.

I'm also sizing a small brass plate for the plinth's front face, adjusting the plinth block heights (bottom and top sections totaling 0.08, turf top at 0.1) so the plate fits proportionally, and updating the trunk base position to match the new turf height.

Now I'm defining a bark texture function for the eucalyptus trunk, using noise to blend a rough lower section with a smoother peeling limb texture higher up.

Then I'm planning where to attach twigs and foliage along each branch, placing them at varying positions outward, inward, forward, and back.

Writing twig generation code...

I'll blend the downward flow with the twig's own direction so each leaf curls naturally toward its tip, building that per-card flow function so each card's index matches its frame order.

I realize batching per twig would multiply draw calls unnecessarily, so instead I'll precompute all flows into a parallel array and resolve them with a single indexed lookup, keeping triangle counts (~4800 for bent cards) well within budget. Now I'm sketching how to procedurally draw a sickle-shaped leaf texture, curving the outline inward from the base to the tip.

I'm defining the half-width and center-curve functions that shape the leaf's silhouette, plus a color scheme with darker/lighter halves, a light midrib line, and darker edges, parameterized for three tinted leaf variants. I also need a smaller tuft texture with triangular spikes, and I'm deciding to skip fuzzy eucalyptus blossoms in favor of keeping the gumnuts, while planning to scatter fur-tuft cards across the koala's body using normal and position filtering.

I'm working out how to tint grey-only tuft textures using a single color or paint sampled at each card's root point, so the fur card color matches the body's local paint color — drawing the base texture in white-to-grey tones with a darker streak, since tinting multiplies and can't lighten beyond the base color. Then I'm setting up the scatter hits to generate card instances from this texture.

Beyond that, I'm skipping fur tufts on limbs except small patches, finalizing eyes and brows with no whiskers, and working out a pixel-stepped outline for the ears using rows of half-widths at a texel size small enough to hit the target ear diameter, adjusting cell size and row counts to get the right proportions.

Settling on 10 rows with widths 6,8,10,10,10,10,10,10,8,6, giving a rounded ear shape roughly 0.12 units tall and wide, built with stepped spans anchored at the bottom origin.

Still defining fur layers...

I'm thinking about scattering small cream-colored tufts around the ear rim, placing them at calculated angles so they sit evenly along the circular edge.

I'll bind them to the ear joint bone so they move rigidly together, then move on to coloring the claws a light cream tone and setting up the jaw as a separate bone-driven part.

For eye placement, I'm mapping decal positions onto the skull surface using azimuth and elevation angles computed from the relative eye offset to the skull center, mirroring the azimuth sign for the opposite side.

Writing head paint function...

Now I need to set up the limb chains using the IK helpers, computing arm points between shoulder and wrist targets with bend hints.

I'm naming the joints per side (shoulder/elbow/wrist with L/R suffixes) and feeding the polyline into the chain builder, then I'll move on to sweeping skin geometry over these chains.

Next I'm sketching out a palm capsule for the hand fur and a reusable `digit` function that builds a two-joint chain per finger, sweeps a tube around it, and optionally adds a claw at the tip.

I need the center point passed in since it's known from the enclosing function. Now I'm sketching a grip function signature taking side, parent, and other options, then writing out the full implementation.

Writing grip function logic...

Setting up the ankle joint and foot pad geometry, then sweeping the leg chain along its path with tapering radius. Adding a small tail nub joint near the hips with a flattened fur-toned sphere at the rump.

Now defining export metadata (name, description, style, commit), then setting up texture parameters for parts and building a skin layout for the nose using pixel texture drawing onto designated face rectangles.

I'm sketching the nose pixel pattern across its faces, using transparent corner pixels so alpha-testing carves away the box corners into a rounded nose silhouette.

Now I'm defining the color palette and a pixel texture helper, then designing a small mouth decal texture with a philtrum line and a simple smile curve beneath the nose.

Next I'm figuring out the wood plank texture tiling for the stand — working out plank dimensions in texels so that larger faces display the tile with stretched but still-square texels, scaling appropriately across the different box faces.

Only showing a sliver of wood texture, so I'm rethinking the plinth approach: instead of tileBox cropping, I'll use cellPaint to procedurally paint wood grain directly onto the box cells, with noise-based ramp coloring stretched along the grain axis plus periodic plank-seam lines and bolt details. That sidesteps the texel-cropping problem entirely, though I still need to figure out whether skinBox is needed elsewhere, like the nose.

For the plinth I'm adding chamfered edges using two stacked inset boxes, corner feet, small dark nail-dot boxes at plank ends, and gold L-shaped brass corner brackets at the top. I'm also planning sweeping tree roots using catmull curves radiating from the trunk base across the turf, tapering from thicker to thinner radius with painted bark, plus setting up the skull geometry with low-poly sphere scaling and a jaw joint definition.

Now I'm deciding the head joint placement and orientation, then moving to compose the sweep geometry for limbs and body — leaning toward flat-faceted shading for limbs and body versus smooth for spheres, balancing the pixel-art dithered paint look against the low-poly faceted geometry for retro clarity. I'm also setting up branch sweeps on both sides using a radius function tied to the base bone.

For the trunk, I'm defining the sweep path and radius taper with a flared base, adding a fork crotch sphere, and planning peeling bark strip textures along the branches plus dark knot discs for texture detail, followed by gathering twig placement seeds per branch.

Now I'm working out twig geometry — attach points along each branch with outward/up/random-z directions, building a bezier curve function for the twig path, then placing eucalyptus-style lanceolate leaf pairs at intervals along each twig with outward-facing card frames and downward droop. I'm also figuring out overall twig density per branch plus some bridging canopy twigs connecting the tops.

Writing the pixel builder setup...
